g3.29a.summary: Lawfare, 10 March 2025: “AI-Generated Voice Evidence Poses Dangers in Court”, by Rebecca Wexler, Sarah Barrington, Emily Cooper and Hany Farid. The rule is spoken, not printed: Federal Rule of Evidence 901(b)(5), an opinion identifying a voice, which has made familiarity a proxy for authenticity for two centuries. The authors’ own research found listeners perceived an AI voice as the same as its real counterpart about 80% of the time and correctly identified a voice as AI-generated only about 60% of the time. Note what they actually argue, which is on the face of the artifact: not that voice evidence be excluded, but that listener authentication should be permissive rather than mandatory, giving judges more discretion.

g3.29b.summary: An explainer from the legal-services firm completelegal.us reporting two proposals working through the Judicial Conference’s Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules: proposed Rule 707, which would treat machine-generated evidence offered without a supporting expert the way Rule 702 treats expert testimony, requiring it to meet reliability standards before admission; and proposed Rule 901(c), the deepfake objection, which turns on a party making a credible claim that evidence was fabricated by AI. Nobody yet knows what a “credible claim” is, who bears the burden, or what stops the objection being routine. Attribution note: cite the Advisory Committee as the authority on stage, not the blog. m1.07.summary: The same paper’s own account of the experiment, in the authors’ own typography: “In less than 6 hours after starting on our in-house server, our model generated 40,000 molecules that scored within our desired threshold”, and the highlighted continuation — the AI designed VX and other known chemical warfare agents it had not been given, plus many new molecules predicted to be more toxic still. The mechanism is the inversion: they did not build a weapons model, they took a commercial toxicity model whose job is to steer away from toxic compounds and flipped the sign on the objective. LD50 maximised and LD50 minimised are the same instruction. Honest hedge the authors themselves make: designing a molecule on paper is not synthesising one — the claim is about the collapse in the cost of the design step, not about manufacture.

s29.summary: A close-up photograph of a skin lesion with a ruler held beside it, and no caption on the slide by design — the reveal is spoken. The story is one of machine learning’s oldest cautionary examples: a lesion classifier appeared to predict malignancy, but what it had actually learned was that clinicians reach for a ruler to measure a lesion when they already suspect cancer, so “ruler” became the feature. It was never looking at the lesion. No specific paper is cited on the slide, so attribute it as a well-known early result rather than to a named study.
